claims.text: An integrated electron–phonon transport model can predict the total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr from 100 to 1200 K within approximately 10% of experiment.
The integrated model will outperform Debye-based or purely lattice-focused approaches.
The relevant simpler approaches exclude defect scattering or do not separately represent electronic and lattice conduction channels.
The modeled alloy is equimolar HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen has a nominally single-phase BCC microstructure.
BCC microstructures are representative of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed calculation uses ab initio phonon dispersions, electron scattering, and a supercell containing realistic defects, particularly oxygen.
Oxygen point defects and local lattice distortions modify phonon scattering paths.
Oxygen point defects and local lattice distortions modify electron scattering paths.
Ab initio force constants and electron–phonon coupling calculations in a representative supercell can accurately account for these defect-mediated scattering effects.
Explicitly decomposing electronic and lattice heat transport while including defect scattering captures the interplay between the two conduction channels.
The model will predict total thermal conductivity within approximately 10% at temperatures at or below 200 K and at or above 1000 K.
Simpler models commonly have thermal-conductivity discrepancies of 20–30%.
Earlier estimates lumped together or neglected electron–phonon contributions, relied on a single Debye temperature, or assumed perfect oxygen-free microstructures.
Earlier estimates often miss experimentally observed thermal-conductivity trends.
Experimental total thermal conductivity is 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
The proposed model is applicable to near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Higher impurity contents, multiphase states, or temperatures above 1200 K may introduce metallurgical or phase-stability effects outside the model scope.
Local inhomogeneity and higher impurity content may change the relative magnitudes of lattice and electronic heat transport.

A systematic deviation greater than approximately 10% anywhere from 100 to 1200 K at approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, or a directly measured contradiction of the predicted channel contributions, would falsify the hypothesis.
